title: Update LLM policy?
body: ## How can Bevy's documentation be improved? I would like to preface this by saying I am neither a lawyer nor an expert on Bevy's policies, and I think a lot of incredible work has been done in this project. However, I am seeking clarification specifically on what appears to be a violation of the LLM policy. One great thing about this project is its no-LLM policy, described [here](https://bevy.org/learn/contribute/policies/ai/): > Erring on the side of caution in light of a openly debated legal topic, all[^1] forms of AI-generated contributions cannot be merged into repositories maintained by the Bevy Organization. This includes both code and non-code game assets (e.g. textures, audio, etc). and later on: > Trivial LLM generated content such as variable renames or autocompleted function calls, often branded "predictions" or "suggestions", that is otherwise indistinguishable from traditional methods such as a regex search/replace or an LSP autocompletion is by definition not detectable and can be treated like other regular IDE tools such as Intellisense. This does not include cases where the prediction generates things like entire function blocks. However, when looking at the Bevy repository today, I was surprised to see that an LLM-generated PR was merged. You can tell at a glance by blocking the `claude` user (although GitHub does not permit blocking Copilot, and this strategy does not handle any unattributed LLM use): Consider [this pull request](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/pull/23276) (which attributes claude as a coauthor) and its [discussion](https://discord.com/channels/691052431525675048/691052431974465548/1481439759040512196) on the Bevy discord. From what I understand, the policy as accessed on 3/18/26 10 PM EST would not permit this PR, which adds an entire function: > This does not include cases where the prediction generates things like entire function blocks. I believe there may be something I am misunderstanding. I would also be interested if anyone knew the latest commit to Bevy known to have no code attributed to LLMs.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: This is unrelated to the actual issue, so it can probably be hidden as off-topic, but in general I am increasingly saddened by how willing projects are to accept LLM-generated or LLM-assisted contributions, from `vim` to `curl` to `rust-analyzer`. It would be great if Bevy would adopt an even stronger policy that requires all contributions to be human-driven; although a human (nonspecific) may (or may not) have written code to solve a bug found by an LLM, this (nonspecific) contribution does not bring in a contributor with a deeper understanding of the codebase, it just brings in potential technical debt.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
My understanding when I merged that PR was that the code was hand-authored, but the investigation was performed with the help of Claude. As such, I felt that it was consistent with the AI policy as written. I was not aware of the "Co-authored by" annotation, but would have inquired as to the exact meaning had I noticed at the time. It is entirely believable that this commit was marked as co-authored out of a sense of professional courtesy.

You are welcome to fork from the commit just before that, or simply remove that commit from your own fork.

Unfortunately, as we do not possess an oracle, we cannot definitively say whether or not any given commit was or was not written by an LLM. Concealing this is trivial, as is adding annotations that are indicative of LLM-generated work. We cannot definitively say, for either legal or ethical reasons, that even without this commit, all of Bevy's code is LLM free.

We also do not possess any control of the contribution policies of our upstream dependencies (including Rust itself), many of which may allow the inclusion of LLM-generated code.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: For want to think about or discuss exactly what our policy should be, here is a carefully written document summarizing diverse perspectives on the use of AI in the [Rust project](https://nikomatsakis.github.io/rust-project-perspectives-on-ai/intro.html) that may be useful.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> Unfortunately, as we do not possess an oracle, we cannot definitively say whether or not any given commit was or was not written by an LLM. Concealing this is trivial, as is adding annotations that are indicative of LLM-generated work. We cannot definitively say, for either legal or ethical reasons, that even without this commit, all of Bevy's code is LLM free.

I think you're describing the difference between having a policy vs. enforcing the policy. I think it depends on what you think a policy should be; I think there are only two options:
- Policies are wholly enforceable
- Policies only reflect values

In particular, I don't think that a policy which is sometimes enforceable is useful because it leads to issues like these.

In the case of LLMs, there is no way to enforce any ban because it is trivially hidden by bad actors. Nevertheless, projects have for years maintained policies to ban bad actors, [including Bevy](https://bevy.org/learn/contribute/policies/code-of-conduct/). I would argue that because there is no way to enforce an LLM ban, the policy should either:

- Not state that there is an LLM ban with a series of exceptions that are not rigorously defined. (enforceable)
- Fully ban all contributes from or assisted by LLMs/other probabilistic models with the understanding that enforcement can only take place in cases where attribution exists. (values)

I don't think a middle-ground policy is effective because $$\{\text{unattributed LLM contributions}\} \subseteq \{\text{unattributed LLM contributions}\} \cup \{\text{attributed LLM contributions}\}$$ and a "middle-ground" policy is simply allowing for some nonempty $\{\text{attributed LLM contributions}\}$ without affecting $\{\text{unattributed LLM contributions}\}$. That is, unless the policy is the strictly enforceable "We allow for LLM contributions as long as X,Y,Z" where X,Y,Z represent provable things.

TL;DR I think either the policy should be entirely enforceable (in which case it cannot mention banning LLMs in the general case) or it should be allowed to fully express project values (in which case it is not bound to realism).

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> Consider [this pull request](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/pull/23276) (which attributes claude as a coauthor) and its [discussion](https://discord.com/channels/691052431525675048/691052431974465548/1481439759040512196) on the Bevy discord. From what I understand, the policy as accessed on 3/18/26 10 PM EST would not permit this PR, which adds an entire function:

I approved that PR, and I completely missed at the time that Claude was a co-author. Just discovered it due to this issue.

> I believe there may be something I am misunderstanding.

Mistakes happen. As you mention, the policy is hard to enforce, it needs either hyper vigilance from the maintainers, witch hunts by the community, or constantly adding new automated controls / CI checks / ... for the latest way to detect each LLM in a non ending chase.

Most people working on Bevy are volunteers, and don't want to spend time checking every PR for LLM contributions. At least that's definitely not the first thing I think of when reviewing a PR. We also want a welcoming community and don't want to be suspicious of every new contributors. Sure in this case it was easy as they marked Claude as co-author, but I personally don't look at committers details, and having multiple co-author is frequent in this repo as we encourage people to share attributions with those that helped.

I don't have a solution, I would be happy if you have one that doesn't involve general suspicion, more time to review each PR or adding each week new automated controls for the latest flavour.

> I would also be interested if anyone knew the latest commit to Bevy known to have no code attributed to LLMs.

The parent commit of the PR you linked, so https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/commit/1c203b6f39a4d8b4e025539e60a266dd0e1a37e3

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I just checked the PR myself, and looking over it and what I understand from the description and the code itself, _it's fine_. It would pass the sniff test as a contribution. It's not great that now we have the "taint" of LLM code, it's so far one commit, and at the very least, if anything breaks as a result of this contribution, we can justify reverting it both from practical and policy reasons. It won't remove the fact we have a Claude co-author, but not much we can do about it.

The easiest *start* to this problem is really just to surface the AI policy and make it more visible. This was a new contributor, so we could just put a notice in the New Contributor welcoming comment to review the AI policy alongside the link to the contributing guide. That is the quickest way to signal to new contributors what our values are. It won't stop those acting in bad faith, but I'm assuming most are acting in good faith and surfacing this information to them quicker will alleviate most of these issues without imposing undue burden on maintainers.
